source.title: Residential Interior Design - A Guide to Planning Spaces

coverage_audit.notes: Full Chapter 1 processed as rendered pages plus extracted text: printed pages 1-28, input pages 1-28, master pages 15-42. Every page was reviewed for text, tables, figures, captions, legends, callouts and dimension lines. Master page numbers were derived from the input file name suffix 15-42, which matches the page count exactly; this derivation is flagged in the review queue. Three internal inconsistencies were found and preserved rather than corrected: the 2015 dwelling area metric equivalency (245 versus 254 m2), the Figure 1-6 caption metric value 118 mm against the dimension line 1118 mm, and the IRC E3901.2.1 metric value 1289 mm against 6 ft. No page was unreadable.

top_findings.why_useful: IRC minimum habitable room area of 70 sq ft (6.5 m2) with no plan dimension under 7 ft (2134 mm) is the hardest floor available for generated room footprints.
Sloped ceiling rule turns ceiling height into a usable-area computation rather than a single height test, which matters for attic and loft rooms.
Glazing at 8 percent and openable ventilation at 4 percent of floor area tie window sizing directly to room area.
Hall personal-casual band of 0.5 to 1.2 m is the proxemic target for sizing conversation groups, and the source explicitly links casual interaction to it.
Shows that a nominal 32 in door yields only 30 in of clear passage, forcing an explicit separation of door leaf width from clear width in the vocabulary.

chapter_summary.notes: Chapter 1 is an introductory chapter, so a large share of its content is conceptual: proxemics, territory and privacy theory, sustainability policy, lighting fundamentals and drawing conventions. Hard numeric material clusters in three places: IRC requirements for habitable rooms, accessibility and visitability heights and widths, and Hall proxemic distance bands. All records are SOURCE_CANDIDATE only. HARD_CANDIDATE was used sparingly and only for cited IRC code minima whose applicability gate (habitable space, one- and two-family dwellings, 2015 edition) is explicit in the source; every recommendation, preference or typical value was kept below that level.

records.concept: Figure 2-3 water/ice management: water, melting snow and ice must be diverted away from the entrance walkway; in the improved examples roof water is diverted by a gutter and downspout, or by the roof configuration itself. records.concept: Figure 2-3 wind rules: prevailing winds vary by region and should always be considered (shown left to right in the figure). Storm doors are necessary in cold regions but are subject to being a high-wind hazard if no protection is built in, and a storm door swing orientation that faces the prevailing wind raises the risk of the door being wind-whipped. An open porch shelters from above but not from wind; a modest-sized recessed porch shelters from both rain/snow and prevailing winds; a projecting, column-supported roof over the stoop does little for wind protection although the storm door swing may still avoid the prevailing wind.
records.rule_plain_language: Orient the entrance and the storm-door swing relative to prevailing wind; recessed porches shelter from wind, open and projecting ones do not.

records.concept: The primary entrance door can create a sense of place and convey meaning about the design and inhabitants; its style should work within the building's design context. Physical qualities matter: whether the door is solid or partly glazed, its relative size and width, and adjoining elements such as sidelights or transom all contribute to the design integrity of exterior and interior. Storm doors, needed in harsh climates, and most screen doors cover the entry door and alter its visual qualities. The entry door should not look like an afterthought or detract from the building's character, should be easy to identify as the primary entrance, and should be reasonably easy to open and move through.

records.concept: Elevators, spiral stairs and ladders require the smallest footprint and generally involve little or no horizontal movement, so the traveller arrives directly above or below the starting point; stairs and ramps can move the traveller a considerable horizontal distance, for example from one side of the house to the other. A switchback stair or ramp (also known as scissor stairs) more closely emulates a spiral stair, because the traveller ends up approximately above or below where they started.
records.rule_plain_language: Horizontal displacement per storey is the discriminator: elevators, spiral and switchback stairs land you above/below the start, straight runs and ramps move you across the plan.

records.concept: Generally speaking, ramps are seldom used in the interiors of a residence except for small vertical changes, or where the design of the house is centred on movement (for example a linear house that cascades down a hillside with the ramp as its spine); ramps consume significant space and are therefore largely relegated to the exterior, where there is more space.

records.concept: Stair terminology: treads are the horizontal upper surfaces where the foot is placed; risers are the vertical or near vertical face of a step; the edge of a tread that extends over the riser is the nosing or nose. The nosing is often rounded, which makes it less likely to catch feet, decreases the risk of tripping and is more comfortable in contact with the body. The sum of all treads is the total run of the stair and the sum of all risers is the rise.
records.rule_plain_language: Vocabulary: tread, riser, nosing, run (sum of treads) and rise (sum of risers); rounded nosings reduce tripping.

records.concept: Figure 2-11c item 2, spiral stairs: the steepest of the legal residential stairs, covered in IRC Section R311.7.10.1. Risers can be as much as 9 1/2 inches (241 mm), with 9 inches (229 mm) shown; the minimum width is 26 inches (660 mm). The number of risers must be sufficient, and each of sufficient height, to create adequate headroom of 6 feet 6 inches minimum (1982 mm) within three-fourths of a circle, so the user does not hit their head on the landing above, which almost always occupies one-fourth of the full circle. records.concept: Vertical movement on stairs can be hazardous: it would be an unusual person who has never had a fall of some sort on a stair, thousands of people are hospitalised each year in the United States for accidents occurring on stairs and thousands more are injured without hospitalisation, so safety should be a significant consideration in stair design. One safety rule of thumb is that the steeper the ascent and descent, the more risk is involved, which makes ladders more dangerous than stairs.

records.concept: One- and two-step stairs can prove as hazardous as multiple steps, not because one falls as far but because fewer steps are more difficult to see, and the most dangerous steps are the ones you do not see. Such configurations need not be avoided but require strong visual cues to the user, which can be provided through a change of flooring materials, the sloping appearance of handrails, a change of colour/texture/materials and adequate lighting.

records.concept: Figure 2-13 items B, C, D and E define the measurement conventions: the riser dimension is taken from tread surface to tread surface; the sum of all the risers is the rise of the stair, which is the floor-level-to-floor-level or landing-to-landing dimension, worked in the caption as 5 risers at 7 3/4 inches (196 mm) equalling 3 feet 2 3/4 inches (984 mm); the tread dimension is the horizontal measurement from nose to nose, which renders the tread surface almost always larger; and the sum of all tread dimensions equals the run of the stair, worked as 4 treads at 10 inches (254 mm) equalling 3 feet 4 inches (1016 mm).

records.concept: The current code minimum in a residential setting is 36 inches (914 mm) wide for a hallway or stair. However, this is not optimal, as persons meeting in such a space will have to pause, slow down and possibly turn sideways; on stairs one person may need to wait at the head or foot for the other to complete the trip. records.concept: The typical stair user can handle a larger riser on the ascent, while a smaller riser would be desirable on the descent; the ideal but impractical stair would have larger risers for the ascent and smaller ones for the descent, requiring two sets of steps. Anecdotally people are frequently seen climbing a stair two risers at a time and often without railing support, but rarely descend two steps at a time and even more rarely without a handrail. Therefore a compromise is struck in favour of the descent, which is inherently the more hazardous: the feet are in much more stable positions on the ascent, and if a fall occurs the person falls into the plane of the stair, a relatively short trip.
records.rule_plain_language: Riser and tread proportions are set for the descent, which is the more dangerous direction, even though ascent could tolerate steeper steps.

records.concept: Figure 2-20 is a set of negative, bad-practice examples. The stairs shown occupy prime real estate within the home, including exterior walls that might be better used for exterior exposure and windows giving light and air to the interior of the house. records.concept: Figure 2-28 illustrates spiral stairs that meet the minimum requirements of the IRC, the example shown being for a 9-foot (2743-mm) floor-to-floor height, with floor-to-floor height varying by residence design. Item A: the stair shown illustrates the code minimum tread width spiral stair, and all tread widths must be identical. Item B: all risers are identical and must be no more than 9 1/2 inches (241 mm); the IRC requires a tread depth of not less than 6 3/4 inches (171 mm) at the walkline of travel; minimum headroom of 6 feet 6 inches (1982 mm) is required for this type of stair, per Section R311.7.10.1. The caption also notes that for clarity and ease of drawing balusters are not shown, but are required similar to straight-run stair requirements.
records.rule_plain_language: Code-minimum spiral stair: identical treads and risers, riser at most 241 mm, tread at least 171 mm at the walkline, headroom 1982 mm, balusters required.

records.concept: The design of ramps is similar to the design of stairs in terms of the need and standards for handrails and for landings at the top, bottom and where ramps change direction, the minimum landing being 3 by 3 feet (914 by 914 mm) per Section R311.8. There is a significant difference between what is allowed for ramps in public accommodations versus private residences in terms of slope, width, length and landing size. In residential use, ramps serving a required egress door must meet the 1:12 slope requirement. The amount of space consumed by a ramp, the footprint, should not be underestimated: it will be significant, and the designer should take that reality into account in the initial stages of the design process.
records.rule_plain_language: Ramps follow stair logic for handrails and landings, need 914 by 914 mm landings at every end and turn, and must be 1:12 when serving a required egress door.

records.concept: Lighting for circulation spaces varies greatly based on the type of space involved. For example, decorative lighting for an elegant open stair located in or near an entry foyer may be supplied by a chandelier and layered with additional ambient light provided by wall sconces or adjustable downlights. On the other hand, lighting in more utilitarian circulation spaces may be provided without decorative fixtures and supplied instead by recessed downlights, surface- or ceiling-mounted luminaires, or cove- or soffit-mounted fluorescent fixtures.
records.rule_plain_language: Match the fixture family to the space: chandelier plus layered sconces or adjustable downlights at a feature stair, recessed or surface luminaires in utilitarian circulation.
records.possible_remlab_interpretation: Selection rule keyed to whether the circulation space is a feature or a service route.

records.concept: Given the range of types of circulation spaces within most houses, careful consideration of desired aesthetic effects as well as the use and requirements of each space must occur. Great drama may be provided in some foyer and entry areas and hallways through the use of chandeliers, pendant fixtures and wall sconces, and many such spaces with higher-than-standard ceilings call for this kind of decorative lighting. In some homes long hallways serve as gallery spaces, and these are well served by accent lighting in addition to general or ambient lighting. In other cases hallways and other circulation spaces may benefit from a simple approach that provides adequate light levels for safe passage with minimal visual impact. This points to the need to establish specific lighting design criteria for circulation spaces, noting visual or aesthetic requirements alongside the basic functional requirement of adequate lighting for safe passage and the architectural parameters.
records.rule_plain_language: Higher-than-standard ceilings in foyers and halls invite decorative fixtures; gallery hallways need accent light on top of ambient; elsewhere aim for safe passage with minimal visual impact.

top_findings.why_useful: The 2R + T = 25 in (610-660 mm) proportioning formula is the single most generative rule in the chapter: it ties riser and tread together for any stair a generator produces, and the chapter supplies worked examples at both ends of the legal band.

The accessibility checklist collects the four numbers that govern accessible circulation in one place: 813 mm clear at doors, 914 mm paths, 1524 mm turning circle or T-turn, and ramp or elevator in place of stairs.

Separates the legal minimum corridor width (914 mm) from the functional one, by stating explicitly that two adults cannot pass at the minimum and that public buildings use 1118-1219 mm. This is the clearest hard-versus-soft threshold pair in the chapter.
Converts ceiling height into floor-to-floor height via a 305 mm floor structure assumption, which is the bridge a generator needs between room parameters and the rise a stair must resolve.

States that one- and two-step level changes are as hazardous as full flights because they are hard to see, and lists the visual cues that mitigate this. It is a rare example of a safety rule that applies to level changes too small to trigger stair code.

All records are SOURCE_CANDIDATE; nothing in this package is a production RemLab rule. Local duplicates are marked with local_duplicate_of and retained rather than merged, because the repeated statements sit in different sections and carry different code citations. Local conflicts are cross-linked and never averaged: the 3658 mm versus 3734 mm landing spacing, and the three spiral-stair footprints. No cross-chapter comparison was performed. 107 records use relation_type=other because the chapter's claim is a property of a single element rather than a relation between two entities; for these, proposed_relation_type was derived from what the record quantifies (element_dimension_specification, element_slope_specification, element_footprint_specification, element_count_specification, or element_design_guidance where the record carries no measurement). Sofa-to-table clearance with an explicit conditional minimum, one of the few genuinely hard candidates.
Per-person occupancy envelope for upholstered seating, needed before any cluster geometry can be validated.
Conversation cluster diameter, the geometric core of the chapter's seating logic.
IRC ceiling height and beam clearance minimums, hard constraints independent of furniture.

top_findings.why_useful: Splits the combined kitchen aisle into a 914 mm work zone plus a 610-762 mm circulation zone totalling at least 1524 mm, and pairs with R018/R019 to give a complete conditional set of aisle minimums driven by through traffic and cook count.

The North American stock cabinet size grid (9 in start, 3 in steps to 24 in, 6 in steps to 48 in; 12 in wall and 24 in base depths) lets generated cabinet runs snap to purchasable sizes rather than arbitrary widths.
The 32 mm frameless system-hole grid with 5 mm holes governs hinge, slide and front positions and is the one genuinely metric modular grid in the chapter.
Asymmetric landing space at the primary sink (610 mm one side, 457 mm the other, both at sink height) is the template for the appliance landing-space family that runs through R069, R090 and R100.
NKBA storage frontage tied to kitchen floor area and to a 1829 mm radius from the sink centre is an unusual quantity-of-storage rule that can be evaluated directly against a generated layout.

chapter_summary.notes: Segment of Chapter 4 (Kitchens) covering printed pages 87-114: appliance clearances and ergonomics, wheelchair-accessible dimensions, dining surfaces, sinks, dishwashers, ranges and cooktops, hoods, ovens and microwaves, refrigerators, kitchen storage zones, the full stock cabinet size tables, cabinet construction, pantries, related IRC/FHAA/UFAS code items, electrical provision and lighting including California Title 24. Every measurement keeps the source's imperial value as value_original with the source's printed metric equivalent recorded in conversion_note; normalization to cm is computed from the imperial value, and eight internal conversion inconsistencies in the source are flagged rather than corrected. All status values are SOURCE_CANDIDATE; no production rule decisions have been made.

coverage_audit.notes: The segment contains no tables; tables_checked records that the pages were inspected for tables and none are present. The figures are raster line drawings with hand-lettered dimensions that do not exist in the PDF text layer, so all dimension strings were read from the page images. Chapter number 4 is taken from the figure numbering (4-35 to 4-53) and the chapter title from the running head. segment_total is null because the number of segments the chapter will be cut into is not known.

records.concept: Mandatory through traffic across the work triangle should be avoided
records.rule_plain_language: Kitchens work best when major circulation routes lie outside the kitchen and no route is forced through the work triangle; where a plan cannot avoid it, alternate routes to adjoining spaces should be created. records.possible_remlab_interpretation: Penalise circulation paths that intersect the work triangle; reward alternate routes around it.

records.concept: Dish storage belongs at the cleanup centre, close to the dishwasher
records.rule_plain_language: Dish storage is repeatedly located in wall cabinets at the cleanup centre, convenient to the sink and dishwasher. records.possible_remlab_interpretation: Adjacency preference: dish storage near dishwasher/sink; fallback to drawer storage when wall cabinets are limited.

records.concept: Degrees of openness between kitchen and adjoining spaces, and their consequences
records.rule_plain_language: Openness is treated as a spectrum with real costs on both ends. records.possible_remlab_interpretation: Daylight quality per work centre depends on glazing position; couples directly to the wall-cabinet trade-off record.

records.concept: Storage and work surfaces placed over or behind appliances are inaccessible
records.rule_plain_language: Negative examples are criticised because work space sits behind the refrigerator and over a range, a wall cabinet over the range is difficult to access, base cabinet storage is inaccessible, and one storage location is relatively inaccessible because it requires reaching over a hot range.
records.possible_remlab_interpretation: Access penalty for storage or work surfaces whose approach passes over a cooking appliance or behind a tall appliance.

records.concept: Aisle width reduced by a projecting appliance, and corridors wider than useful
records.rule_plain_language: A main aisle that is already minimal is reduced further by a refrigerator projecting into it. At the other extreme, a 5 foot 6 inch width is called wider than necessary: it gains little beyond adding steps and partially accommodating through traffic.
records.possible_remlab_interpretation: Effective aisle width must be measured to the face of the deepest projecting appliance, not to the cabinet line.

top_findings.why_useful: Explicit min/typical/max band for the work corridor between opposing runs (42 / 48 / 60 in), one of the few quantified clearance rules in the segment.

Stool spacing at 27 in on centre and a stated required minimum knee space of 15 in at eating bars.
The chapter's most repeated trade-off: openness and glazing cost wall-cabinet storage, which must be compensated by pantry and drawer storage.

coverage_audit.notes: Input was received as rendered page images together with the embedded PDF text layer, hence input_mode=MIXED. The chapter contains no true tables; all dimensional data is carried in figures, so tables_checked reflects that no table content was found rather than that tables were present and read. Figure content was read from captions, numbered notes and the embedded text of dimension labels. No value was read off drawing scale and no illegible digit was reconstructed by inference. Four specific figure items could not be read with confidence and are recorded as REFERENCE_ONLY with needs_verification rather than excluded: the perimeter dimension lines of Figure 5-7, the sliding-door panel sub-ranges of Figure 5-11, the printed metric area of closet c1 in Figure 5-12, and the imperial-only dimensions of Figure 5-19d. Item counting method: relevant_source_items_mapped_to_records equals the count of evidence objects across all records, since each evidence object localises one distinct source item; the same source item cited by two records is counted once per record and this is a known over-count of at most a few items.

records.concept: The location of the bedroom entrance relative to exterior walls (and therefore windows) is a primary determinant of room form. The authors identify four basic bedroom form types: A — one exterior wall opposite the entrance; B — two exterior walls, one opposite the entrance, producing a corner room; C — one exterior wall adjacent to the entrance, less common because it requires a hallway to terminate at the bedroom entrance; D — entrance flanked by three exterior walls, a bedroom wing offering daylight on three sides but limiting closet placement to the single location adjacent to the entry door.
records.rule_plain_language: Four bedroom form types follow from how the entrance sits relative to exterior walls; the type constrains where closets, windows and furniture can go.
records.possible_remlab_interpretation: Classification layer that should precede furniture placement; each type carries different closet and glazing options.

top_findings.why_useful: Bed-side clearance for bed making is the single most reusable hard geometry in the chapter, and the source cleanly separates the functional minimum from the comfortable target.
Area-to-capability threshold: it converts a room area directly into how many walls can carry furniture, which is exactly the decision a layout solver makes first.
Storage front clearance is object-state dependent (drawer open vs closed), a distinction that a naive footprint model would lose entirely.
Closet-to-entrance adjacency with an explicit frequency rationale, and it implies a traffic path from entry to closet that does not pass the bed.
One of the very few quantified efficiency relationships in the chapter: double loading yields 27 percent more rod per square foot of closet area.

chapter.title: Bathrooms

coverage_audit.notes: Input was processed as page images together with the embedded text layer, so figure dimension strings (Figures 6-3a/b, 6-4, 6-5, 6-7, 6-13a/b, 6-15, 6-17, 6-23a/b, 6-24a) were read from the figures themselves rather than reconstructed from body text. No true tables appear in this segment; tables_checked records that the segment was searched for them. The dense sink, tub and shower size figures carry graphic axis labels only, so width versus depth assignment there is marked medium confidence and flagged for verification rather than asserted. No dimension was read off by scaling a drawing. Master page numbers are derived from the input file name range 162-183 (offset +14 from printed pages); see the review queue.

top_findings.why_useful: Separates the recommended minimum shower size (36 by 36 in) from the IRC P2708.1 code minimum (30 by 30 in) and records the sub-minimum 2 ft 8 in case, giving RemLab two distinct thresholds instead of one blended number.

Gives a directly generative vanity constraint: at least 24 in of cabinet width at any sink location, with top drawers omitted across that width, plus an explicit not-recommended band at 15 in and below.
A measurable seated-reach band of 15 to 48 in above the floor for bathroom storage and accessories, attributed to NKBA and tied to an explicit user context.
The only explicit minimum clear floor space in the segment (30 by 60 in at an accessible tub), together with the companion features the IDEA Center requires alongside it.
A genuinely conditional code rule where a dimensional relaxation to 25 in is valid only when total stall area reaches 1300 square inches, a shape RemLab cannot represent as a plain minimum.

top_findings.why_useful: The bathroom equivalent of a work triangle: rules of thumb that order sink, toilet and bathing fixtures relative to the entry door, giving RemLab a placement sequence rather than only isolated clearances.
Standard toilet clear zone with both minimum and recommended width and depth, and with the bounding element generalized to 'fixture, wall or door' - directly usable as a clearance primitive.
IRC P2705 gives the code floor (381 mm centreline, 533 mm in front) beneath the more generous recommended values elsewhere in the chapter, so RemLab can distinguish hard constraints from preferences.
A rare explicit parametric relationship: a second sink increases room area by 35 percent, which supports program sizing rather than only conflict checking.
Shower door swing direction is conditional on stall size, an example of a genuine conditional rule that must not be flattened into a constant.

top_findings.why_useful: 36 in (914 mm) minimum circulation and work space in front of the washer and dryer is the single most directly applicable clearance in the chapter for a laundry zone.
IRC requirement that an appliance receptacle sits within 6 ft (1829 mm) of the appliance is a checkable distance constraint between a service point and an appliance position.
Code-derived keep-out volume in front of an electrical service panel, a hard constraint candidate for any utility room that hosts the panel.
Activity-specific work surface height: 28 in (711 mm) for sewing against 36 in (915 mm) for laundry work, showing that counter height must follow the activity rather than the room.
Zone-to-room area ratio (stretching zone at roughly 25-50 percent of the gym floor area) is a rare proportional rule usable directly as a soft layout constraint.

records.concept: Windows are categorized by how they open: sliding vertically (double-hung, where both sashes slide, and single-hung, where only the bottom sash slides), sliding horizontally (sliding), and hinged to open outward (casement hinged at the side, awning hinged at the top, hopper hinged at the bottom); transom windows are fixed and used in the top position in combination with other types.

top_findings.why_useful: Fireplace placement must enhance the room without impeding traffic flow or making the room difficult to furnish - a direct scoring criterion for generated layouts.
Central door placement divides a room in half while corner placement pushes circulation to the edges and frees the interior for furniture groups.
Window placement should support multiple furniture layouts rather than a single one - directly applicable to layout generation and evaluation.
Floor material transitions belong directly under the closed door leaf - an unambiguous geometric rule for finish boundaries.
Door swings should land against a blank wall and must not overlap circulation or other swings - a checkable opening-envelope constraint.

top_findings.why_useful: The only true dimensional data in the chapter: typical front (20-40 ft) and side (6 ft) setbacks and a proportional rear setback, which bound the footprint of any addition.
States that circulation, organizational flow and clearances must be re-checked whenever space is added or rearranged, linking the remodeling workflow to the room-level clearance rules held elsewhere.
Attic conversion is gated on a required minimum ceiling height that this chapter names without a value: an explicit gap to fill from a codes chapter during merge.
A clean conditional gate: a basement may become a bedroom only with appropriate egress and ventilation.
Defines the wall-surface-to-wall-surface convention for overall room dimensions, which normalises how measured-survey inputs should be read.

chapter_summary.notes: Chapter 10 is a process chapter about planning remodeling work, not a room-dimension chapter. It contains almost no ergonomic or clearance figures: the only spatial dimensions in the whole chapter are the typical zoning setbacks in R089. Most numeric content is economic (2015 US cost-vs-value tables and budget shares) and is kept as REFERENCE_ONLY because it is dated, national-average market data rather than design guidance. Several genuine constraints are named without values (attic minimum ceiling height, lot coverage, maximum height, required parking count, allowable floor area); these are kept with null measurement values and needs_verification rather than dropped or filled from general knowledge. Two raster images exist in the input, both photographs (Figures 10-1 and 10-2); there are no dimension lines, plans or dimensioned diagrams anywhere in the chapter.
